{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=artificial+agency+reward+attribution+models+moral+responsibility+theoretical+requirements&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"AGI imagined: social AGI and the co-formation of human-AGI society.\", \"abstract\": \"The AI industry is advancing toward an Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) that will possess cognitive capabilities that are equal to or stronger than those of humans. While a purely computational AGI may be cognitively powerful, it will probably struggle to understand the human social environment. This gap needs both a theoretical and an applicative solution. This article provides the theoretical solution, specifying what such an AGI must contain and how it must be formed. We propose a theoretical construct of an AGI that will not only be computational but will also be capable to develop internal social understanding, internalize norms in a manner similar to humans, and act upon this social understanding. We call such AGI a \\\"Social AGI.\\\" We argue that Social AGI cannot be developed only by using technical alignment or external governance. Instead, it must undergo a staged development in which visible social behavior gradually becomes social cognition and norm internalization. This process cannot be separated from the parallel support that human society must provide the effort of developing Social AGI. While AI systems may become more familiar and embedded in institutions and society itself, the public perceptions of risk will probably decline. This normalization will provide the basis for granting the Social AGI progressively higher levels of autonomy. In order to capture this process of mutual change, we develop a socio-technical concept of human-AGI co-formation. We differentiate co-formation from co-existence, which describes humans and AI operating side by side, and from co-evolution, which describes reciprocal and cyclic influence. Co-formation refers to a process in which at the beginning Social AGI is shaped exclusively by human society. However, as the process progresses, they shape together the basic conditions under which the AGI is developed. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=theoretical+frameworks+for+artificial+moral+agency+and+responsibility+attribution+in+autonomous+systems&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule.
